strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful editing representation: convex 3D primitives provide explicit controls for camera motion, object translation, scaling, rotation, and deletion at multiple abstraction levels.

The projection-based texture-hint mechanism is a sensible use of the inferred geometry and appears to preserve object identity and local appearance better than unconditioned generation or key-value injection in the shown examples.
The method is training-free on the image-generation side and leverages an existing depth-conditioned FLUX model, making the overall approach modular and practically appealing.

The paper is visually clear, includes diverse qualitative examples, reports runtime, gives correspondence algorithms, and candidly illustrates failures involving lighting, decomposition, rotations, and prompt conflicts.
weaknesses: The evaluation is far too limited for the broad claims. The only quantitative comparison uses LooseControl on just 48 images and random camera moves, with no confidence intervals, statistical tests, controlled edit magnitudes, or results for object-level edits. StableFlow and DragDiffusion receive only one or two qualitative comparisons, while several closely related 3D-aware editing methods discussed in the paper are not evaluated.

The quantitative protocol is insufficiently independent and may favor the proposed representation. Geometry is judged using monocular estimated depth after scale-and-shift alignment, while texture is measured using correspondences and confidence masks produced by the authors' own primitive-based pipeline. The paper does not report mask coverage or performance on disoccluded and boundary regions, so difficult pixels may be excluded. Perceptual quality, semantic correctness, edit success, and human preference are not measured.

The demonstrated scope is substantially narrower than the framing suggests. The results primarily edit images generated from the same prompt, noise tensor, and depth-conditioned model. The discussion admits that editing real input images does not currently work well without a suitable inversion method, despite earlier language suggesting primitive extraction and editing from any image.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing or questionable. Depth Anything v2 does not generally provide camera intrinsics, yet focal lengths are essential to the claimed 3D lifting and are not specified. Dataset construction and filtering, train/validation/test splits, optimization objectives and weights, refinement details, grid-search ranges, camera-motion distributions, and random-seed handling are inadequately documented. The reported 40–100 minute training time for separate networks on 1.8M images also requires clarification.

The novelty is moderate: primitive decomposition, depth-conditioned FLUX synthesis, geometric reprojection, and masked latent blending are mostly established components. Their integration is useful, but the texture-warping idea is relatively direct and the paper does not isolate the contribution through comprehensive ablations against ordinary depth warping, alternative masks/inpainting, different primitive fits, or stronger feature-warping methods.

Several central claims are unsupported, including superiority in visual fidelity, editability, and compositional generalization. There is no user study of the proposed interaction model, no systematic decomposition-success analysis across scene categories, and no quantitative evaluation of variable abstraction beyond primitive-to-depth reconstruction error.

The method has consequential limitations for genuine 3D-aware editing: it does not update shadows, reflections, or view-dependent appearance; large rotations fail; thin or non-convex structures are poorly represented; text prompts can override geometric edits; and temporal consistency is absent. These limitations are acknowledged but not characterized quantitatively.

Geometry-based reprojection is a sensible way to construct texture hints, and integrating it with a pretrained depth-conditioned generator avoids retraining the expensive image model.

The qualitative examples cover several primitive counts and edit types, and the paper candidly illustrates meaningful failure modes involving lighting, poor decomposition, rotations, and prompt conflicts.
The appendix provides correspondence algorithms, runtime information, and evidence that increasing the primitive count improves depth approximation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is far too limited to support the central claims of state-of-the-art visual fidelity, editability, and compositional generalization. The sole quantitative comparison uses only 48 images, one main baseline, one primitive count, and random camera moves; object translations, rotations, scaling, deletion, composed edits, and semantic controllability receive no quantitative evaluation.

Baseline coverage is inadequate and uneven. DragDiffusion and StableFlow are compared only on a few selected qualitative examples, while relevant 3D-aware editors discussed in the paper—such as DiffusionHandles, Dragin3D, Image Sculpting, 3D-Fixup, Obj3DiT, OMG3D, and Build-A-Scene—are not experimentally compared. LooseControl lacks an equivalent texture-preservation mechanism, making the large PSNR/SSIM advantage difficult to interpret as a controlled comparison.

The metrics are potentially biased toward the proposed pipeline. DepthAnythingV2 supplies both primitive-training supervision and the estimated depth used for evaluation, while texture consistency is measured using the authors' own primitive correspondences and confidence mask. This can reward agreement with the method's assumptions and exclude difficult or newly visible regions. There is no independent geometric ground truth, perceptual identity metric, human study, or statistical uncertainty.

The paper contains important technical inconsistencies. Its FLUX description uses a variance-preserving diffusion equation and noise prediction even though rectified-flow FLUX is normally formulated with linear interpolation and velocity prediction. The mask equation applies the hint where m is zero despite the text defining m as indicating where the hint should guide generation. Algorithm 2 also skips pixels when the hit mask equals one, contrary to its stated purpose. These issues leave the central implementation ambiguous.

Reproducibility is weak. The 1.8M-image training data construction, filtering, losses, optimization schedule, validation/test splits, camera-motion distribution, prompt set, seed handling, and baseline protocols are insufficiently specified, and no code, models, or benchmark are provided. The reported 40–100 minute training time for separate models over 1.8M images also needs clarification.

The claimed real-image applicability is not demonstrated. The discussion states that successful edits currently require the same prompt and noise tensor used to generate the source, effectively restricting the evaluated system to its own generated images. This substantially narrows the practical scope suggested by the abstract and introduction.

The contribution is largely an integration of existing convex decomposition, conventional 3D texture reprojection, masked latent replacement, and pretrained FLUX depth conditioning. The geometry-derived hint is useful, but the paper does not establish enough methodological novelty or empirical breadth to overcome the evaluation and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and useful contribution: convex 3D primitives form an intuitive, editable intermediate representation for camera motion and object-level translation, scaling, deletion, and rotation. Variable primitive counts also provide a meaningful coarse-to-fine control mechanism. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b01966832dc64b748b98c0634442ee7b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The geometry-aware texture-hint and confidence-mask construction is technically sensible and makes effective use of correspondences unavailable to purely 2D editing methods. Its integration with a pretrained FLUX depth model without generator fine-tuning is practically attractive.

Results show substantial gains over LooseControl on the reported test set: destination AbsRel improves from 0.146 to 0.076, PSNR from 6.65 to 18.7, and SSIM from 0.670 to 0.874. The qualitative results cover several edit types and generally preserve identity and layout convincingly.

The paper is well organized, provides pseudocode for correspondence and hint generation, reports runtime and hyperparameter choices, studies primitive counts, and candidly illustrates failure modes involving lighting, decomposition errors, rotations, and prompt conflicts.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation contains only 48 images with random camera motions and compares against just one method. It lacks uncertainty estimates, a human preference study, systematic object-edit evaluation, and quantitative comparisons with other relevant editing systems such as StableFlow, DragDiffusion, DiffusionHandles, Build-A-Scene, Image Sculpting, or OMG3D. The isolated qualitative comparisons are insufficient to establish broad state-of-the-art performance.

The evaluation protocol may favor the proposed representation: the authors supply their primitives to both methods, use a DepthAnything-family estimator after training primitive predictors from DepthAnythingV2 supervision, and compute texture scores through their own primitive-derived correspondence and confidence mask. Independent geometry metrics, segmentation-based object-placement measures, perceptual identity metrics, and evaluation masks not produced by the proposed pipeline would strengthen the evidence.

The framing sometimes suggests editing arbitrary input images, but the experiments focus on images generated using the same prompt and noise tensor; the discussion acknowledges that real-image editing still requires a suitable inversion method. This materially narrows the demonstrated applicability and should be reflected more explicitly in the main claims.

The novelty is partly an integration of existing convex decomposition, geometric reprojection, and a pretrained depth-conditioned generator. The precise algorithmic advances over the decomposition methods in references 47 and 49 are not sharply isolated, and ablations do not separately quantify refinement, the confidence mask, Voronoi filling, hint timing, or StableFlow integration.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a system trained on 1.8 million LAION images: dataset selection and filtering, training losses, optimizer and schedule, validation composition, test-set construction, and release plans for code, models, prompts, seeds, and edit parameters are not adequately specified.

The exposition of FLUX as rectified flow appears technically inaccurate: the stated variance-preserving forward equation and noise-prediction formulation do not match the usual linear interpolation and velocity prediction of rectified-flow models. There is also apparent ambiguity in Algorithm 2 about skipping pixels for which the hit mask equals one. These issues may be expository rather than implementation errors, but they should be corrected.

Important limitations remain for holes and thin structures, cluttered or boundary objects, large rotations, view-dependent illumination and shadows, prompt-edit conflicts, and temporal consistency. Collectively, these prevent the current evidence from supporting an OA of 8, although the core contribution is sufficiently promising for a marginal accept.

strengths: The primitive-based interface is intuitive and supports object/part translation, scaling, rotation, deletion, and camera motion at variable levels of detail.

The projection-based texture hint and confidence mask are sensible uses of the explicit 3D representation, with qualitative examples showing better identity preservation than generation from depth alone.
The paper is visually clear, candidly presents several failure modes, and includes useful ablations of hint timing, mask dilation, primitive count, and depth-conditioning strength.
Runtime information, pseudocode, hyperparameters, and extensive supplementary examples provide a reasonable starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are insufficiently supported. The main quantitative comparison uses only 48 images and one baseline, LooseControl; object and part edits are evaluated primarily through selected qualitative examples. Strong relevant methods listed in the related-work matrix, including Diffusion Handles, DragIn3D, FlowDrag, and editable image elements, receive no substantive empirical comparison.

The evaluation metrics are partly self-referential and incomplete. Geometry is judged using a monocular depth estimator with per-image scale-and-shift alignment rather than actual edited geometry, while texture is measured only on visible regions using correspondences and masks produced by the proposed representation. This favors texture copying and does not assess disocclusions, newly synthesized content, overall realism, or semantic correctness.

Claims of superior visual fidelity, editability, and compositional generalization are substantially stronger than the evidence. There is no user study of interface quality or perceptual realism, no systematic compositional-generalization protocol, and no quantitative evaluation of requested object/part transformations.

It is unclear how broadly the method works on arbitrary real photographs. Many demonstrations appear to use images generated within the authors' pipeline, and the discussion states that successful edits should share the source prompt and initial noise tensor—information unavailable for ordinary photographs. This conflicts with the broad input-image framing and needs a dedicated real-image evaluation.

The novelty is moderate: the system combines an existing convex-decomposition approach, a pretrained depth-conditioned FLUX model, and conventional 3D reprojection/nearest-neighbor texture transfer. The texture-hint integration is useful, but its technical advancement is limited relative to the breadth of the claims.

Reproducibility and responsible-use reporting remain incomplete: the training objective and data-processing pipeline rely heavily on prior work, release plans are unspecified, and the use of 1.8M LAION images is not accompanied by discussion of filtering, licensing, privacy, bias, or misuse risks. strengths: The use of editable convex 3D primitives provides an intuitive, explicit interface for object, part, and camera manipulation, with variable primitive counts supporting different editing granularities.

The geometry-based texture-hint and confidence-mask mechanism is a sensible integration of 3D correspondences with a pretrained depth-conditioned FLUX model. The reported ablations indicate that this mechanism substantially improves texture consistency over generation without hints and over StableFlow.

The paper contains many qualitative examples, useful hyperparameter ablations, runtime information, and a candid discussion of several failure modes, including lighting inconsistencies, poor decomposition, and rotation artifacts.
The results are visually promising for selected translations, scaling operations, and modest camera changes, and the system appears practically useful when its primitive decomposition is accurate.
weaknesses: The central superiority claims are not supported by a sufficiently broad or rigorous evaluation. The main quantitative comparison uses only 48 images and one baseline, LooseControl, while comparisons with DragDiffusion and proprietary systems are anecdotal. Relevant methods such as Image Sculpting, DragIn3D, FlowDrag, Build-A-Scene, and other explicit-3D editors are discussed but not empirically compared.

The metrics are partly self-referential and favor the proposed representation. Geometry is evaluated by comparing rendered primitive depth against monocular depth estimated from the output, with scale-and-shift fitting; texture is evaluated through correspondences and visibility masks generated by the authors' own primitive pipeline. These measurements do not directly establish edit accuracy, perceptual realism, or preservation of object identity.

There is no human evaluation of the claimed intuitiveness, editability, visual fidelity, or identity preservation. Likewise, the claimed compositional generalization is illustrated through selected examples but is not quantitatively defined or evaluated.

Baseline fairness is unclear. LooseControl receives primitives produced by the proposed system despite having been designed for a different conditioning distribution, and the DragDiffusion comparisons depend on manually chosen drag points without a documented protocol, multiple-run statistics, or controlled effort budget.

The methodological novelty is moderate: the pipeline largely combines an existing convex-decomposition method, conventional 3D texture reprojection and nearest-neighbor inpainting, and an off-the-shelf depth-conditioned FLUX model. The paper does not clearly isolate which contribution goes beyond this integration.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the long appendix. Essential details are missing, including the primitive-training losses, LAION sampling and filtering, train/validation/test splits, camera-intrinsic assumptions, test-time refinement settings, random seeds, sample counts for several supplementary experiments, and a code or model-release commitment. Some mask definitions and pseudocode are also difficult to reconcile with the stated update equations.

The experiments appear dominated by selected or generated source images. Robustness on a clearly defined, diverse benchmark of real photographs is not demonstrated, even though the method is presented as accepting arbitrary images.

The acknowledged failures are central to general-purpose 3D-aware editing: clutter can merge objects, non-convex shapes are poorly represented, large rotations distort geometry and text, lighting and reflections remain fixed, prompt conflicts produce residual objects, and composed edits weaken texture preservation.

Training ten separate primitive predictors on 1.8 million LAION images is a substantial dependency that weakens the framing of the overall approach as training-free. Dataset provenance, licensing, potential biases, and image-manipulation risks receive no meaningful ethical discussion.

strengths: Presents a clear and useful interaction paradigm: editable, variable-resolution 3D convex primitives provide explicit control over object translation, scaling, rotation, deletion, and camera motion.
The projection-based texture-hint and confidence-mask mechanism is technically well motivated and exploits the primitive geometry effectively to preserve appearance across edits.
Results show large improvements over LooseControl in the reported camera-move evaluation, while ablations demonstrate that the proposed hint is responsible for substantial texture-consistency gains.

The paper includes extensive and generally compelling qualitative examples, meaningful failure cases, runtime information, algorithm pseudocode, and ablations of hint timing, depth-conditioning strength, primitive count, and mask dilation.
The method combines existing primitive decomposition and pretrained FLUX components in a novel, coherent pipeline without requiring task-specific retraining of the image generator.

The paper is visually clear, well positioned against several categories of related work, and candid about limitations such as lighting inconsistency, poor decomposition, prompt conflicts, and large-rotation artifacts.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evaluation is limited: Table 1 uses only 48 images and compares against a single baseline, LooseControl. Stronger related methods listed in the paper, including DragIn3D, Diffusion Handles, FlowDrag, GoodDrag, and mesh-based editors, receive no controlled quantitative comparison.

Important experimental details are underspecified, including how the 48 test scenes and random camera moves were selected, the source and diversity of the evaluation images, the transformation ranges, seed handling, and whether hyperparameters were fixed before test evaluation. Statistical uncertainty is absent from the principal comparisons.

The evaluation metrics do not fully establish semantic edit success or perceptual quality. Texture scores are measured only over geometrically corresponding visible pixels and directly favor methods that inject the source warp; no human study, preference evaluation, identity metric, or artifact-sensitive assessment complements them.

Geometry evaluation depends on estimated depth from the same DepthAnything family used to supervise primitive training and applies scale-and-shift fitting, creating possible estimator coupling and potentially masking absolute geometric errors. Evaluation using independent depth estimators or scenes with ground-truth geometry would be more convincing.

Claims of superior editability and compositional generalization are stronger than the evidence: editability is not assessed through user studies, interaction time, selection accuracy, or task completion, while compositional edits are mainly demonstrated qualitatively and are acknowledged to degrade texture fidelity.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not state that code, trained primitive models, evaluation splits, prompts, transformation parameters, and random seeds will be released; training losses and refinement details also rely substantially on prior work.

The method requires separately trained predictors for many primitive counts and 1.8M LAION images, which weakens the simplicity and “training-free” framing despite the paper's clarification that only generation is training-free. Dataset filtering, licensing, bias, and misuse considerations for realistic image manipulation are not discussed.
